newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission merger powers face crucial test.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission merger powers face crucial test.

text.p: The European Commission faces a crucial legal test later this year that could force it to scrap some of its highest-profile merger decisions, including the 1996 ban of the platinum merger between Gencor Ltd and Lonrho Plc.

The European Union's competition watchdog has throughout this decade banned or set strict conditions on corporate mergers and takeovers that would leave the affected markets at the mercy of two or three players -- so-called duopolies or oligopolies.

The legal basis for doing this was shaky and the controversial decisions could backfire if the European Court of Justice concludes that the Commission has overstepped the powers granted by the EU's merger control law.
The ruling is expected before the end of the year, possibly in the autumn, court officials said.
Among the companies eagerly awaiting the decision is South African mining giant Gencor which was barred from merging its platinum interests with those of British conglomerate Lonrho.
Anglo American Corp, another South African mining firm, is equally interested in the ruling since the Commission ordered it earlier this year to cut its stake in Lonrho to less than 10 percent.

Although separate, the decisions were based on an identical assumption: that two of the three companies that control the supply of platinum worldwide would no longer compete against each other, resulting in a duopoly.

The problem is that the EU's merger regulation, which in 1990 turned the Commission into a one-stop regulatory shop for large mergers and acquisitions affecting the Union, allows actions only to prevent the creation or strengthening of dominant positions.
The Commission believes the law also applies to situations where a small number of companies dominate the market even though it does not explicitly say that.

But Court advocate general Giuseppe Tesauro disagreed, advising the European judges in February to scrap the conditions attached in 1993 to the acquisition by German potash producer Kali & Salz BASF, a unit of BASF.F, of troubled east German rival MdK.

"The Commission's argument that the absence of a provision that expressely excludes applying the regulation to positions of collective dominance implies that the question was left open does not appear convincing to us," his opinion said.

The Commission's decision was challenged by French potash company EMC and its distributor SCPA, whose close links with Kali were severed as a result of the concessions obtained from the German company.
According to the Commission, Kali/MdK and SCPA/EMC would together have accounted for 80 percent of Europe's production of potash, one of three nutrients used to make agricultural fertilisers.
COURT COULD LEAVE QUESTION OPEN

In the majority of cases brought before its jurisdiction, the court follows the opinion of its advocates general. But some lawyers suspect that the Court in this case may sidestep the question of whether the bloc's 1990 merger regulation applies to corporate deals that create oligopolies.

"I think the court would be very cautious in any circumstances, but certainly here where it would be overturning a policy which has been adopted by the Commission and applied already in several cases," said Stephens Spinks, a partner with U.S. law firm Coudert Brothers.
"They might follow the advocate general's opinion, but I think they will look very carefully before they do so," Spinks added.

"I cannot imagine that the Court follows the advocate general in this case...but it may also find a way to leave the question open," said Horst Satzky from German law firm Hengeler, Mueller, Weitzel, Wirtz.
A third lawyer, Charles Price, from Price, Blanpain, Quaghebeur, speculated that the Court may scrap the conditions imposed on the Kali & Salz/MdK case without ruling on the legal issue.
"The Court may dodge the question. It does not have to decide on this to annul the Commission's decision," he said.

A fudge would win only a respite, however, since Gencor has also taken the Commission to Court over last year's decision on the Lonrho merger, arguing in part that the merger regulation does not cover oligopolies.

Because of the legal challenges, some of the national antitrust experts sitting on a committee which advises the Commission on merger control have become very nervous about continuing to back the Commission on similar decisions.

In 1995, a minority expressed concern about attaching conditions to a rail joint venture between the Swiss-Swedish engineering group ABB and Daimler-Benz which the Commission's competition services thought would give the new company and Siemens joint dominance in the markets for trams and metro vehicles in some countries.

"A minority...feels that there are doubts regarding the application of the regulation to situations of collective dominance and that pending a decision by the Court of Justice on the Kali/MdK appeal, it is not clear whether the Commission is legally in a position to control such situations at this stage," said the opinion published in the EU's Official Journal earlier this year.
This minority view was expressed in other merger opinions, including that on the aborted Gencor/Lonrho deal.

In the absence of a clear Court ruling, the Commission may have to ask the governments of the 15 EU states to revise the merger regulation -- an uphill struggle considering their recent reluctance to extend the Commission's powers over mergers and acquisitions.
Advocate-general Tesauro said that in his opinion that would be more in keeping with "the rules of the game" than trying to introduce new powers through the back door.
